claim: IRAK2 is an atypical kinase due to amino acid substitution of key catalytic residues (Asp -> Asn333; Asp ->His351).
source: IRAK2 is an atypical kinase due to the amino acid substitution of key catalytic residues (Asp -> Asn333; Asp ->His351 Figure 1A)
evidence: The manuscript directly states this structural feature and references Figure 1A showing the structural model.

claim: Recombinant wild-type IRAK2 can autophosphorylate and phosphorylate myelin basic protein (MBP).
source: While the purified recombinant wild-type IRAK2 was able to autophosphorylate and phosphorylate myelin basic protein (MBP), the IRAK2 mutants (KK235AA and H351A) displayed minimum activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1B demonstrates IRAK2 kinase activity.

claim: IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (KK235AA, H351A, and N333A) display minimum kinase activity.
source: While the purified recombinant wild-type IRAK2 was able to autophosphorylate and phosphorylate myelin basic protein (MBP), the IRAK2 mutants (KK235AA and H351A) displayed minimum activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay results shown in Figure 1B demonstrate reduced activity of mutants.

claim: Wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive mutants, restores LPS-mediated induction of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in IRAK2-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Wild-type IRAK2, but not IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA; catalytic site mutants H351A and N333A), restored LPS-mediated induction of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in IRAK2-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages (Figure 1C and E)
evidence: ELISA data in Figure 1C and Western blot in Figure 1E show restoration of cytokine production only with wild-type IRAK2.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is necessary for ligand-induced pro-inflammatory gene expression.
source: Wild-type IRAK2, but not IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA; catalytic site mutants H351A and N333A), restored LPS-mediated induction of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in IRAK2-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages (Figure 1C and E), suggesting that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is necessary for ligand-induced pro-inflammatory gene expression.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing that only kinase-active IRAK2 restores inflammatory responses.

claim: LPS-induced production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines was greatly reduced in macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice compared to wild-type control mice.
source: LPS-induced production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines was greatly reduced in the macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice compared to that of the wild-type control mice (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: ELISA data in Figure 1D and Western blot in Figure 1F demonstrate reduced cytokine production in kinase-inactive knockin mice.

claim: IRAK2 is modified in bone marrow-derived macrophages in response to LPS stimulation.
source: Notably, IRAK2 is modified in bone marrow-derived macrophages in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 1E shows a modified form of IRAK2 after LPS treatment.

claim: Wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive mutants, restores IRAK2 modification in IRAK2-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Wild-type IRAK2, but not IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA; catalytic site mutants H351A and N333A), restored IRAK2 modification in IRAK2-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages (Figure 1E).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1E shows modification only with wild-type IRAK2.

claim: The modified form of IRAK2 is translocated into the nucleus in a ligand-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, we found that the modified form of IRAK2 was translocated into the nucleus in a ligand-dependent manner (Figure 1F).
evidence: Nuclear fractionation and Western blot in Figure 1F shows nuclear localization of modified IRAK2 after LPS treatment.

claim: IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (KK235AA, H351A, and N333A) fail to translocate into the nucleus.
source: Immunofluorescent staining showed that IRAK2 ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA and catalytic site mutants (H351A and N333A), failed to translocate into the nucleus, suggesting that IRAK2 kinase activity is important for its nuclear translocation (Figure 1G).
evidence: Confocal imaging in Figure 1G shows cytoplasmic localization of kinase-inactive mutants.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is important for its nuclear translocation.
source: Immunofluorescent staining showed that IRAK2 ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA and catalytic site mutants (H351A and N333A), failed to translocate into the nucleus, suggesting that IRAK2 kinase activity is important for its nuclear translocation (Figure 1G).
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that kinase-inactive mutants fail to translocate to the nucleus.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation was abolished in macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.
source: In support of this, LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation was abolished in the macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: Nuclear fractionation data in Figure 1F shows no nuclear IRAK2 in kinase-inactive knockin macrophages.

claim: Oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL), TLR7 ligand R848, and TLR9 ligand CpGB stimulation can induce IRAK2 modification and nuclear translocation.
source: Interestingly, not only LPS stimulation leads to IRAK2 modification and nuclear localization, endogenous TLR4 ligand oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL), TLR7 ligand R848 and TLR9 ligand CpGB stimulation can also induce IRAK2 modification and subsequent nuclear translocation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 shows IRAK2 modification and nuclear localization with multiple TLR ligands.

claim: IRAK2 contains a putative nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the kinase domain (Aa 357–366: HPDNKKTKYT).
source: Nuclear localization signal (NLS) is a short peptide motif that mediates the nuclear import of proteins by binding to importin complex. We identified a putative NLS in the IRAK2 kinase domain (Aa 357–366: HPDNKKTKYT), which was mutated by substituting the three lysine residues (K361, K362 and K364) with alanines.
evidence: The manuscript describes identification of a putative NLS sequence based on known NLS characteristics.

claim: IRAK2 NLS mutant fails to translocate into the nucleus.
source: Immunofluorescent staining showed that the IRAK2 NLS mutant indeed failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Confocal imaging in Figure 1G shows cytoplasmic localization of NLS mutant.

claim: IRAK2 NLS mutant fails to restore LPS-induced inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production in IRAK2-deficient macrophages.
source: IRAK2 NLS mutant also failed to restore LPS-induced inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production in IRAK2-deficient macrophages (Figure 1C and E), indicating that IRAK2 nuclear translocation is required for IRAK2-mediated inflammatory gene expression.
evidence: ELISA data in Figure 1C shows no restoration of cytokine production with NLS mutant.

claim: IRAK2 nuclear translocation is required for IRAK2-mediated inflammatory gene expression.
source: IRAK2 NLS mutant also failed to restore LPS-induced inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production in IRAK2-deficient macrophages (Figure 1C and E), indicating that IRAK2 nuclear translocation is required for IRAK2-mediated inflammatory gene expression.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that NLS mutant cannot restore inflammatory responses.

claim: IRAK2 NLS mutant fails to be modified.
source: While we showed that modified IRAK2 was translocated into the nucleus (Figure 1F), IRAK2 NLS mutant failed to be modified (Figure 1E), implicating a critical link between IRAK2 nuclear translocation and modification.
evidence: Western blot in Figure 1E shows no modification of NLS mutant.

claim: There is a critical link between IRAK2 nuclear translocation and modification.
source: While we showed that modified IRAK2 was translocated into the nucleus (Figure 1F), IRAK2 NLS mutant failed to be modified (Figure 1E), implicating a critical link between IRAK2 nuclear translocation and modification.
evidence: The link is inferred from the observation that NLS mutant is not modified and cannot translocate.

claim: IRAK2 interacts with importin-β.
source: Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis showed that IRAK2 interacts with importin-β (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Mass spectrometry data identified importin-β as an IRAK2-interacting protein.

claim: IRAK2 forms a complex with RanBP2.
source: Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis showed that IRAK2 interacts with importin-β (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and co-immunoprecipitation experiment implicates the formation of IRAK2-RanBP2 complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A shows IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction.

claim: IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (KK235AA, H351A, N333A) retain interaction with importin-β.
source: We found that IRAK2 ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA and catalytic site mutants H351A/N333A retained the interaction with importin-β, whereas NLS mutant failed to form a complex with importin-β (Figure 2A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A shows importin-β binding to kinase-inactive mutants.

claim: IRAK2 NLS mutant fails to form a complex with importin-β.
source: We found that IRAK2 ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA and catalytic site mutants H351A/N333A retained the interaction with importin-β, whereas NLS mutant failed to form a complex with importin-β (Figure 2A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A shows no importin-β binding to NLS mutant.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is not required for IRAK2's NLS to engage the importin complex.
source: We found that IRAK2 ATP-binding site mutant KK235AA and catalytic site mutants H351A/N333A retained the interaction with importin-β, whereas NLS mutant failed to form a complex with importin-β (Figure 2A). These results suggest that the IRAK2 kinase activity is not required for IRAK2's NLS to engage the importin complex.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that kinase-inactive mutants still bind importin-β.

claim: IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutants (KK235AA, H351A, N333A) and NLS mutant lose interaction with RanBP2.
source: On the other hand, IRAK2 KK235AA and H351A/N333A kinase-inactive mutants and as well as NLS mutant lost interaction with RanBP2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A shows no RanBP2 binding to these mutants.

claim: LPS stimulation induces phosphorylation of IRAK2 at S136 and T140.
source: It has been reported that LPS stimulation induces the phosphorylation of IRAK2 at S136 and T140 (Weintz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication.

claim: Mutation at IRAK2 phosphorylation sites S136A/T140A abolishes LPS-induced interaction of IRAK2 with RanBP2.
source: We found that mutation at these two phosphorylation sites (IRAK2 S136A/T140A double mutant) abolished LPS-induced interaction of IRAK2 with RanBP2 and its nuclear localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows no RanBP2 binding to S136A/T140A mutant.

claim: Mutation at IRAK2 phosphorylation sites S136A/T140A abolishes LPS-induced nuclear localization of IRAK2.
source: We found that mutation at these two phosphorylation sites (IRAK2 S136A/T140A double mutant) abolished LPS-induced interaction of IRAK2 with RanBP2 and its nuclear localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Confocal imaging in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows cytoplasmic localization of S136A/T140A mutant.

claim: IRAK2 S136A/T140A double mutant retains interaction with importin-β.
source: We found that mutation at these two phosphorylation sites (IRAK2 S136A/T140A double mutant) abolished LPS-induced interaction of IRAK2 with RanBP2 and its nuclear localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), although the IRAK2 S136A/T140A double mutant still retained the interaction with importin-β.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows importin-β binding to S136A/T140A mutant.

claim: Activation of IRAK2 results in auto-phosphorylation at S136A and T140A, which mediates interaction with RanBP2.
source: These findings suggest that the activation of IRAK2 may result in auto-phosphorylation at S136A and T140A, which in turn mediates the interaction with RanBP2.
evidence: The mechanism is inferred from the observation that phosphorylation site mutants lose RanBP2 interaction.

claim: The modified form of IRAK2 is specifically co-immunoprecipitated by RanBP2.
source: In support of this, it is indeed the modified form of IRAK2 was specifically co-immunoprecipitated by RanBP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows RanBP2 preferentially binds modified IRAK2.

claim: Phosphorylated IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBP2.
source: Furthermore, the phos-tag gel electrophoresis confirmed that the phosphorylated IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBp2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Phos-tag gel analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows phosphorylated IRAK2 binds RanBP2.

claim: RanBP2 carries an active SUMO E3 ligase domain.
source: Notably, the C-terminal of RanBP2 carries an active SUMO E3 ligase domain, which was shown to modulate cytoplasmic and nuclear transport of macromolecules (Pichler et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication.

claim: IRAK2 is characterized as a sumoylated protein in a recent proteomics study.
source: Importantly, IRAK2 is characterized as a sumoylated protein in recent proteomics study (Lamoliatte et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication.

claim: LPS stimulation induces the interaction between IRAK2 and RanBP2.
source: LPS stimulation indeed induced the interaction between IRAK2 and RanBP2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2B shows LPS-induced IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction is abolished in macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.
source: We found LPS-induced IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction was abolished in the macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice (Figure 2B), confirming that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is required for its interaction with RanBP2.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2B shows no IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction in kinase-inactive knockin macrophages.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for its interaction with RanBP2.
source: We found LPS-induced IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction was abolished in the macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice (Figure 2B), confirming that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is required for its interaction with RanBP2.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that kinase-inactive IRAK2 does not bind RanBP2.

claim: IRAK2 is conjugated by SUMO1 in response to LPS stimulation.
source: Furthermore, SUMO1 was detected in IRAK2 immunoprecipitates under denaturing condition, these results indicate that IRAK2 is conjugated by SUMO1 in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation under denaturing conditions in Figure 2C shows SUMO1 conjugation to IRAK2.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation is abolished in macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.
source: Consistent with the fact that IRAK2 kinase-inactive mutant failed to interact with RanBP2, LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation was abolished in the macrophages from IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2C shows no SUMO1 conjugation in kinase-inactive knockin macrophages.

claim: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant loses sumoylation.
source: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant lost sumoylation, and failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2D shows no SUMO1 conjugation to K123/182/592R mutant.

claim: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant fails to translocate into the nucleus.
source: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant lost sumoylation, and failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Confocal imaging in Figure 2E shows cytoplasmic localization of K123/182/592R mutant.

claim: IRAK2 sumoylation plays an essential role for IRAK2 nuclear translocation.
source: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant lost sumoylation, and failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that IRAK2 sumoylation plays an essential role for IRAK2 nuclear translocation.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that sumoylation-deficient mutant cannot translocate to the nucleus.

claim: Wild-type IRAK2 is sumoylated in vitro by RanBP2.
source: By in vitro sumoylation assay, we found that wild-type IRAK2 was sumoylated, whereas the K123/182/592R triple mutant failed to be modified (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: In vitro sumoylation assay in Figure 2F shows IRAK2 sumoylation by RanBP2.

claim: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant fails to be sumoylated in vitro.
source: By in vitro sumoylation assay, we found that wild-type IRAK2 was sumoylated, whereas the K123/182/592R triple mutant failed to be modified (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: In vitro sumoylation assay in Figure 2F shows no sumoylation of K123/182/592R mutant.

claim: The modified form of IRAK2 disappears after treatment with SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1.
source: The modified form of IRAK2 disappeared after treatment with SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1, confirming the observed modification of IRAK2 was indeed due to sumoylation (Figure 2G).
evidence: Western blot in Figure 2G shows loss of modified IRAK2 band after Ulp1 treatment.

claim: The observed modification of IRAK2 is due to sumoylation.
source: The modified form of IRAK2 disappeared after treatment with SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1, confirming the observed modification of IRAK2 was indeed due to sumoylation (Figure 2G).
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that Ulp1 treatment removes the modification.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation is abolished in the absence of RanBP2.
source: To further assess the importance of RanBP2 in LPS-induced IRAK2 modification, RanBP2 was knocked down in macrophages. LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation was abolished in the absence of RanBP2, confirming that RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation (Figure 2H).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2H shows no IRAK2 sumoylation in RanBP2 knockdown cells.

claim: RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation.
source: To further assess the importance of RanBP2 in LPS-induced IRAK2 modification, RanBP2 was knocked down in macrophages. LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation was abolished in the absence of RanBP2, confirming that RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation (Figure 2H).
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that RanBP2 knockdown abolishes IRAK2 sumoylation.

claim: The sumoylated form of IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBP2.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiment showed that the sumoylated form of IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows preferential binding of sumoylated IRAK2 to RanBP2.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation is abolished in RanBP2 knock-down cells.
source: Furthermore, LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation was abolished in RanBP2 knock-down cells, supporting the critical role of IRAK2 sumoylation for its nuclear translocation (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Nuclear fractionation data in Figure 2I shows no nuclear IRAK2 in RanBP2 knockdown cells.

claim: IRAK2 sumoylation plays a critical role for its nuclear translocation.
source: Furthermore, LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation was abolished in RanBP2 knock-down cells, supporting the critical role of IRAK2 sumoylation for its nuclear translocation (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that blocking sumoylation prevents nuclear translocation.

claim: A group of mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) accumulate in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2.
source: We identified a group of mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2, suggesting that IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Microarray analysis in Figure 3A shows nuclear accumulation of these mRNAs in IRAK2 KO cells.

claim: IRAK2 is required for the exportation of Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2 mRNAs.
source: We identified a group of mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2, suggesting that IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that these mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus without IRAK2.

claim: Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2 mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus of IRAK2 kinase inactive macrophages.
source: The same mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) were also accumulated in the nucleus of IRAK2 kinase inactive macrophages, suggesting that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3B).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 3B shows nuclear accumulation of these mRNAs in IRAK2 kinase-inactive macrophages.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for the exportation of Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2 mRNAs.
source: The same mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) were also accumulated in the nucleus of IRAK2 kinase inactive macrophages, suggesting that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that these mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus in kinase-inactive macrophages.

claim: SRSF1 binding sites are significantly enriched in the 3'UTRs of LPS-induced mRNAs that accumulate in the nucleus of IRAK2-deficient macrophages.
source: As a result, we found that the binding sites of SRSF1 (KGRWGSM, K: G/U; R:G/A; W:A/U; S:G/C; M:A/C) are significantly enriched in the 3'UTRs of the positive set (LPS-induced mRNAs that were accumulated in the nucleus of IRAK2-deficient macrophages compared to that in wild-type macrophages) versus the negative set (LPS-induced mRNAs whose cytosol/nuclear distribution in the macrophages was not affected by IRAK2 deficiency), and this motif significantly improves the fitting to the data than ones based on the background distribution (Likelihood ratio test p-value<0.0004) (Figure 3C).
evidence: RNA-READ motif scanner analysis in Figure 3C shows significant enrichment of SRSF1 binding sites.

claim: SRSF1 interacts with IRAK2 in the nucleus.
source: Interestingly, we detected SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction in the nucleus by duo-link assay (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Proximity ligation assay in Figure 3D shows SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction in the nucleus.

claim: SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction is abolished for IRAK2 kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.
source: Interestingly, we detected SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction in the nucleus by duo-link assay (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which was abolished for IRAK2 kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.
evidence: Proximity ligation assay in Figure 3D shows no SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction for kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.

claim: IRAK2 can phosphorylate SRSF1 in vitro.
source: Furthermore, IRAK2 was able to phosphorylate SRSF1 in the in vitro kinase assay (Figure 3E).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay in Figure 3E shows IRAK2 phosphorylates SRSF1.

claim: LPS induces SRSF1 serine/threonine phosphorylation.
source: In support of this, we found that LPS indeed induced SRSF1 serine/threonine phosphorylation, which was diminished in IRAK2-kinase-inactive nucleus (Figure 3F).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3F shows LPS-induced SRSF1 phosphorylation.

claim: LPS-induced SRSF1 phosphorylation is diminished in IRAK2-kinase-inactive nucleus.
source: In support of this, we found that LPS indeed induced SRSF1 serine/threonine phosphorylation, which was diminished in IRAK2-kinase-inactive nucleus (Figure 3F).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3F shows reduced SRSF1 phosphorylation in IRAK2 kinase-inactive cells.

claim: SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form.
source: Previous studies have shown that SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form (Sanford et al., 2005; Xiao and Manley, 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 phosphorylation drives the dissociation of SRSF1 from mRNA targets, promoting their nuclear export.
source: Previous studies have shown that SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form (Sanford et al., 2005; Xiao and Manley, 1997), suggesting that IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 phosphorylation probably drives the dissociation of SRSF1 from the mRNA targets, promoting their nuclear export.
evidence: The mechanism is inferred from known SRSF1 behavior and observed IRAK2-mediated phosphorylation.

claim: SRSF1-bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts are increased in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages compared to wild-type cells.
source: By RNA immunoprecipitation, we indeed found that SRSF1-bound transcripts (Cxcl1 and Tnf) were increased in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages compared to that in wild-type cells (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3G shows increased SRSF1 binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf in IRAK2-deficient and kinase-inactive cells.

claim: IRAK2 directly phosphorylates SRSF1 in the nucleus in response to LPS stimulation, facilitating dissociation of SRSF1 from LPS-induced transcripts and their nuclear export.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that IRAK2 may directly phosphorylate SRSF1 in the nucleus in response to LPS stimulation, which facilitates the dissociation of SRSF1 from the LPS-induced transcripts, and the subsequent nuclear export of these mRNAs.
evidence: The mechanism is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing IRAK2-SRSF1 interaction, phosphorylation, and effects on mRNA export.

claim: SRSF1-bound Ctnnb1 transcript is not affected by LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency.
source: Notably, SRSF1 also plays a critical role in regulating genes that are constitutively expressed, such as Ctnnb1 (β-catenin) (Fu et al., 2013). Interestingly, SRSF1-bound transcript Ctnnb1 was not affected by either LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency (Figure 3G), indicating that IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3G shows no change in SRSF1 binding to Ctnnb1 with LPS or IRAK2 deficiency.

claim: IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
source: Notably, SRSF1 also plays a critical role in regulating genes that are constitutively expressed, such as Ctnnb1 (β-catenin) (Fu et al., 2013). Interestingly, SRSF1-bound transcript Ctnnb1 was not affected by either LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency (Figure 3G), indicating that IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that not all SRSF1-bound transcripts are affected by IRAK2.

claim: ALYREF was identified as an IRAK2-interacting protein by mass spectrometry analysis.
source: Importantly, ALYREF nuclear export factor was actually among the proteins based on MS analysis of IRAK2 immunoprecipitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 identified ALYREF as an IRAK2-interacting protein.

claim: LPS stimulation induces the interaction of IRAK2 with ALYREF in the nucleus.
source: By coimmunoprecipitation, we found that LPS stimulation induced the interaction of IRAK2 with ALYREF in the nucleus (Figure 4A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows LPS-induced IRAK2-ALYREF interaction in the nucleus.

claim: ALYREF interacts with wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.
source: Duo-link assay showed that ALYREF interacts with wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Proximity ligation assay in Figure 4B shows ALYREF interaction only with wild-type IRAK2.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity and sumoylation are required for IRAK2's interaction with ALYREF in the nucleus.
source: Duo-link assay showed that ALYREF interacts with wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1). These results indicate that the kinase activity of IRAK2 and subsequent sumoylation are required for IRAK2's interaction with ALYREF in the nucleus, which is probably due to the fact that the kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 1G).
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants do not interact with ALYREF and do not translocate to the nucleus.

claim: ALYREF is absent in SRSF1 immunoprecipitates.
source: Since LPS-induced the interaction of IRAK2 with SRSF1 (Figures 3D–F and 4A), we wondered whether IRAK2-SRSF1 and IRAK2-ALYREF belong to one complex. Interestingly, ALYREF was absent in the SRSF1 immunoprecipitates, while SRSF1 was also not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates (Figure 4A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows no ALYREF in SRSF1 immunoprecipitates.

claim: SRSF1 is not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates.
source: Since LPS-induced the interaction of IRAK2 with SRSF1 (Figures 3D–F and 4A), we wondered whether IRAK2-SRSF1 and IRAK2-ALYREF belong to one complex. Interestingly, ALYREF was absent in the SRSF1 immunoprecipitates, while SRSF1 was also not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates (Figure 4A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows no SRSF1 in ALYREF immunoprecipitates.

claim: IRAK2 is detected in both SRSF1 and ALYREF immunoprecipitates in response to LPS stimulation.
source: On the other hand, IRAK2 was detected in either SRSF1 or ALYREF immunoprecipitates in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows IRAK2 in both SRSF1 and ALYREF immunoprecipitates.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2's interaction with SRSF1 and ALYREF are mutually exclusive.
source: Interestingly, ALYREF was absent in the SRSF1 immunoprecipitates, while SRSF1 was also not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates (Figure 4A). On the other hand, IRAK2 was detected in either SRSF1 or ALYREF immunoprecipitates in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 4A). These results suggest that LPS-induced IRAK2's interaction with SRSF1 and ALYREF are mutually exclusive.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that SRSF1 and ALYREF do not co-immunoprecipitate but both interact with IRAK2.

claim: LPS stimulation induces the binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf mRNAs.
source: In support of this, RIP analysis showed that LPS stimulation induced the binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to the mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf, and ALYREF's binding to the mRNAs was substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figures 4C-D shows LPS-induced binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to these mRNAs.

claim: ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf mRNAs is substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages.
source: In support of this, RIP analysis showed that LPS stimulation induced the binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to the mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf, and ALYREF's binding to the mRNAs was substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4D shows reduced ALYREF binding in IRAK2-deficient and kinase-inactive cells.

claim: ALYREF-bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts are increased in SRSF1 knock-down cells, even in IRAK2 KO macrophages.
source: Interestingly, ALYREF bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts were increased in SRSF1 knock-down cells, even in IRAK2 KO macrophages, indicating that ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf is no longer IRAK2-dependent in the absence of SRSF1 (Figure 4E and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E shows increased ALYREF binding in SRSF1 knockdown cells.

claim: ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf is no longer IRAK2-dependent in the absence of SRSF1.
source: Interestingly, ALYREF bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts were increased in SRSF1 knock-down cells, even in IRAK2 KO macrophages, indicating that ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf is no longer IRAK2-dependent in the absence of SRSF1 (Figure 4E and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that ALYREF binds target mRNAs in SRSF1 knockdown cells even without IRAK2.

claim: ALYREF-bound Ctnnb1 mRNA is not affected by LPS stimulation, IRAK2 deficiency or SRSF1 knockdown.
source: Similar to SRSF1, ALYREF also binds to constitutively expressed Ctnnb1 mRNA. Importantly, ALYREF-bound Ctnnb1 mRNA was not affected by LPS stimulation, IRAK2 deficiency or SRSF1 knockdown (Figure 4E).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E shows no change in ALYREF binding to Ctnnb1 under various conditions.

claim: The role of IRAK2 for ALYREF's binding to target mRNAs is to remove SRSF1 from the targets.
source: These results confirmed that the role of IRAK2 for ALYREF's binding to the target mRNAs is probably to remove SRSF1 from the targets.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that ALYREF can bind target mRNAs without IRAK2 when SRSF1 is absent.

claim: Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA is efficiently exported to the cytosol in SRSF1 knockdown cells in the absence of IRAK2.
source: Consistently, whereas IRAK2 deficiency resulted in nuclear accumulation of Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA, Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA was efficiently exported to the cytosol in SRSF1 knockdown cells in the absence of IRAK2 (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 4F shows cytosolic localization of Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA in SRSF1 knockdown cells even without IRAK2.

claim: LPS stimulation induces the interaction of IRAK2 with Nxf1.
source: In addition to the LPS-induced interaction of IRAK2 with ALYREF, we found that LPS stimulation also induced the interaction of IRAK2 with Nxf1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A shows LPS-induced IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction.

claim: IRAK2 fails to interact with Nxf1 in the absence of ALYREF.
source: IRAK2 failed to interact with Nxf1 in the absence of ALYREF, suggesting that IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for ALYREF to facilitate the assembly of nuclear export complex to the target mRNAs, including the recruitment of Nxf1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A shows no IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction in ALYREF knockdown cells.

claim: IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for ALYREF to facilitate the assembly of nuclear export complex to target mRNAs, including recruitment of Nxf1.
source: IRAK2 failed to interact with Nxf1 in the absence of ALYREF, suggesting that IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for ALYREF to facilitate the assembly of nuclear export complex to the target mRNAs, including the recruitment of Nxf1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction requires ALYREF.

claim: LPS stimulation induces Nxf1's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNAs in an ALYREF- and IRAK2-dependent manner.
source: In support of this, LPS stimulation induced Nxf1's binding to the mRNAs in an ALYREF- and IRAK2-dependent manner (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figures 5B-D shows LPS-induced Nxf1 binding that is reduced in ALYREF and IRAK2 knockdown/knockout cells.

claim: LPS-induced Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus in the absence of ALYREF.
source: To further assess the importance of ALYREF in LPS-induced IRAK2-dependent mRNA nuclear export, we measured nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA levels in ALYREF knockdown cells. Consistent with the RIP analysis, we found that LPS-induced mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of ALYREF (Figure 5E)
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 5E shows nuclear accumulation of these mRNAs in ALYREF knockdown cells.

claim: ALYREF is important for IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of inflammatory mRNAs.
source: To further assess the importance of ALYREF in LPS-induced IRAK2-dependent mRNA nuclear export, we measured nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA levels in ALYREF knockdown cells. Consistent with the RIP analysis, we found that LPS-induced mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of ALYREF (Figure 5E), indicating the importance of this nuclear export factor in IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of the inflammatory mRNAs.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that inflammatory mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus without ALYREF.

claim: LPS-induced secretion of CXCL1 and TNF is dramatically reduced in ALYREF knockdown cells.
source: By enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analysis, we showed that LPS-induced secretion of CXCL1 and TNF was dramatically reduced in ALYREF knockdown cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: ELISA data in Figure 5F shows reduced cytokine secretion in ALYREF knockdown cells.

claim: SRSF1 binds to Cxcl1 3'UTR (nt 781–901).
source: Using Cxcl1 3'UTR (nt 781–901, which contains stimulus-sensitive motifs (Datta et al., 2010; Hartupee et al., 2007), we validated the SRSF1 binding to this transcript by RNA electrophoretic mobility shift assay (REMSA) (Figure 6A).
evidence: REMSA data in Figure 6A shows SRSF1 binding to Cxcl1 3'UTR.

claim: Nucleotides 800–855 in Cxcl1 3'UTR are important for SRSF1 binding.
source: We identified several putative SRSF1-binding motifs in this region of Cxcl1 3'UTR. Deletion analysis and REMSA showed the importance of nt 800–855 in Cxcl1 3'UTR for SRSF1 binding.
evidence: Deletion analysis and REMSA demonstrate the importance of this region for SRSF1 binding.

claim: SRSF1 binds to luciferase reporter mRNA containing the 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940).
source: While SRSF1 RIP precipitated the luciferase reporter mRNA containing the 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), IRAK2 expression reduced SRSF1 binding to the target mRNA (Figure 6B).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows SRSF1 binding to luciferase reporter with Cxcl1 3'UTR.

claim: IRAK2 expression reduces SRSF1 binding to luciferase reporter mRNA containing Cxcl1 3'UTR.
source: While SRSF1 RIP precipitated the luciferase reporter mRNA containing the 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), IRAK2 expression reduced SRSF1 binding to the target mRNA (Figure 6B).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows reduced SRSF1 binding with IRAK2 expression.

claim: SRSF1 fails to bind luciferase mRNAs with mutated Cxcl1 3'UTR (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835).
source: However, SRSF1 RIP failed to precipitate the luciferase mRNAs with the mutated 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) (Figure 6B).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows no SRSF1 binding to mutated constructs.

claim: IRAK2 strongly promotes luciferase activity from constructs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR (721–940).
source: For the cells transfected with wild-type Cxcl1 luciferase construct (with wild-type 3' UTR of Cxcl1 721–940), IRAK2 strongly promoted the luciferase activity (Figure 6C).
evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6C shows increased luciferase activity with IRAK2 expression.

claim: Cytosolic luciferase reporter mRNAs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR are increased in IRAK2-transfected cells.
source: Consistently, the cytosolic luciferase reporter mRNAs (with wild-type 3' UTR of Cxcl1 721–940) were increased in the IRAK2-transfected cells compared to the cells without IRAK2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 6D shows increased cytosolic luciferase mRNA with IRAK2.

claim: IRAK2 has reduced ability to promote luciferase activity in cells transfected with mutant Cxcl1 luciferase constructs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835).
source: IRAK2 had much reduced ability to promote luciferase activity in cells transfected with mutant Cxcl1 luciferase constructs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6C shows reduced luciferase activity with mutant constructs.

claim: Removal of the functional SRSF1-binding site traps luciferase reporter mRNAs in the nucleus.
source: Removal of the functional SRSF1-binding site trapped the luciferase reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) in the nucleus and IRAK2 can no longer promote nuclear export of these mutant reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) (Figure 6D).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 6D shows nuclear retention of mutant luciferase mRNAs.

claim: IRAK2 cannot promote nuclear export of luciferase reporter mRNAs lacking functional SRSF1-binding sites.
source: Removal of the functional SRSF1-binding site trapped the luciferase reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) in the nucleus and IRAK2 can no longer promote nuclear export of these mutant reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) (Figure 6D).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 6D shows IRAK2 cannot promote export of mutant mRNAs.

claim: SRSF1-binding sequence is required for nuclear export promoted by IRAK2.
source: These results suggest that while SRSF1 binding may sequester the luciferase reporter mRNAs in the nucleus, the SRSF1-binding sequence is actually required for nuclear export promoted by IRAK2.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that IRAK2 cannot promote export of mRNAs lacking SRSF1-binding sites.

claim: LPS stimulation induces luciferase activity from cells transfected with constructs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940).
source: LPS stimulation induced luciferase activity from the cells transfected with constructs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), which was abolished in IRAK2-deficient macrophages (Figure 6E).
evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6E shows LPS-induced luciferase activity with wild-type construct.

claim: LPS-induced luciferase activity from constructs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR is abolished in IRAK2-deficient macrophages.
source: LPS stimulation induced luciferase activity from the cells transfected with constructs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), which was abolished in IRAK2-deficient macrophages (Figure 6E).
evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6E shows no LPS-induced luciferase activity in IRAK2 KO cells.

claim: LPS-induced luciferase activity is substantially reduced in wild-type, IRAK2-deficient or IRAK2-kinase inactive macrophages transfected with mutant luciferase constructs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835).
source: However, LPS-induced luciferase activity was substantially reduced in wild-type, IRAK2-deficient or IRAK2-kinase inactive macrophages transfected with mutant luciferase constructs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6E shows reduced luciferase activity with mutant constructs in all cell types.

claim: IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of target mRNAs is dependent on SRSF1-binding sites in the target mRNA.
source: These results confirm that IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of the target mRNAs is dependent on the SRSF1-binding sites in the target mRNA.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from luciferase assay results showing that mutant constructs lacking SRSF1-binding sites are not exported by IRAK2.

claim: IRAK2 promotes ALYREF binding to wild-type luciferase reporter mRNAs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940).
source: Consistent with the fact that IRAK2 is required for LPS-induced ALYREF's binding to the target mRNAs, IRAK2 promoted ALYREF RIP of wild-type luciferase reporter mRNAs (containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 nt 721–940) (Figure 6F).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6F shows increased ALYREF binding with IRAK2 expression.

claim: ALYREF reduces binding to mutant luciferase reporter mRNAs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) even in the presence of IRAK2.
source: Interestingly, ALYREF reduced the binding to the mutant luciferase reporter mRNAs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) even in the presence of IRAK2 (Figure 6F).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6F shows reduced ALYREF binding to mutant constructs.

claim: The SRSF1-binding site is required for ALYREF's binding to target mRNAs.
source: These results suggest that the SRSF1-binding site seems to be required for ALYREF's binding to the target mRNAs.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that ALYREF binding is reduced when SRSF1-binding sites are deleted.

claim: ALYREF can directly bind to the probe containing the SRSF1-binding site (Cxcl1 nt 800–855) in vitro.
source: In support of this, ALYREF can directly bind to the probe that contains the SRSF1-binding site in the in vitro RNA-binding assay (Cxcl1 nt 800–855, Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: REMSA data in Figure 6G shows ALYREF binding to the SRSF1-binding site probe.

claim: The SRSF1-binding site renders LPS-IRAK2 sensitivity of target mRNA for nuclear export via IRAK2-mediated removal of SRSF1 and recruitment of ALYREF.
source: Taken together, our results implicate that the SRSF1-binding site renders the LPS-IRAK2 sensitivity of the target mRNA for the nuclear export possibly via the IRAK2-mediated removal of SRSF1 and recruitment of nuclear export factors ALYREF to the target mRNAs.
evidence: The mechanism is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing the importance of SRSF1-binding sites for IRAK2-mediated export.

claim: IRAK2 kinase-inactive knock-in mice show substantially increased survival after LPS-induced septic shock compared to wild-type mice.
source: We found that IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice showed substantially increased survival after LPS-induced septic shock compared to that of the wild-type mice (Figure 7A)(Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: Survival curve data in Figure 7A shows increased survival in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.

claim: LPS-induced serum CXCL1 and TNF levels are much reduced in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: Likewise, LPS-induced serum CXCL1 and TNF levels were much reduced in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice compared to that of the wild-type mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: ELISA data in Figure 7B shows reduced serum cytokine levels in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.

claim: LPS/TLR4 engagement activates a nuclear function of IRAK2 that facilitates assembly of nuclear export machinery to export inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for protein translation.
source: In this study, we report that LPS/TLR4 engagement activates a nuclear function of IRAK2 that facilitates the assembly of nuclear export machinery to enable export the inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for protein translation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing multiple experimental findings.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for RanBP2-mediated IRAK2 sumoylation and nuclear translocation.
source: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for RanBP2-mediated IRAK2 sumoylation and nuclear translocation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing that kinase-inactive mutants are not sumoylated and do not translocate to the nucleus.

claim: Nuclear IRAK2 phosphorylates SRSF1 and reduces SRSF1 binding to target mRNAs.
source: Nuclear IRAK2 then phosphorylates SRSF1 and reduces SRSF1 binding to the target mRNAs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from in vitro kinase assays and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: LPS induces interaction between IRAK2 and nuclear export adaptor ALYREF to replace SRSF1 on target mRNAs.
source: At the same time, LPS induces interaction between IRAK2 and nuclear export adaptor ALYREF to replace SRSF1 on the target mRNAs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Recruited ALYREF bridges the interaction between mRNA targets and nuclear export receptor Nxf1, triggering Nxf1 loading for mRNA export.
source: The recruited ALYREF in turn bridges the interaction between the mRNA targets and nuclear export receptor Nxf1, triggering nuclear export receptor Nxf1 loading for the export of the mRNAs. (Figure 7C)
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments showing ALYREF-dependent Nxf1 recruitment.

claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 activation provides a critical check point for production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines by controlling nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution of LPS-induced transcripts.
source: Therefore, LPS-induced IRAK2 activation provides a critical check point for the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines by controlling the nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution of the LPS-induced transcripts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Atypical kinases such as KSR2 and CASK have been reported to carry catalytic activity.
source: Notably, atypical kinases such as KSR2 (Brennan et al., 2011) and CASK (Mukherjee et al., 2008) have been reported to carry catalytic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Mutations in the ATP-binding site and catalytic residues impaired the function of IRAK2.
source: We found recombinant IRAK2 was able to autophophorylate and phosphorylate MBP and SRSF1; mutations in the ATP-binding site and catalytic residues impaired the function of IRAK2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from in vitro kinase assays and functional studies.

claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is critical for the function of IRAK2 in LPS-induced pro-inflammatory response.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the IRAK2 kinase activity is critical for the function of IRAK2 in LPS-induced pro-inflammatory response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing that kinase-inactive IRAK2 cannot restore inflammatory responses.

claim: RanBP2 is a major nucleoporin that extends cytoplasmic filaments from the nuclear pore complex and contains phenylalanine–glycine repeats that bind nuclear transport receptors of the importin beta family.
source: While importin-β is one of the transport receptor mediating translocation of molecules into the cell nucleus, RanBP2 is a major nucleoporin that extends cytoplasmic filaments from the nuclear pore complex and contains phenylalanine–glycine repeats that bind nuclear transport receptors of the importin beta family (Wu et al., 1995; Yokoyama et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Phosphorylation of IRAK2 at S136 and T140 affects its interaction with RanBP2.
source: Our data showed that mutations in putative IRAK2 phosphorylation sites S136/T140 (Weintz et al., 2010) substantially reduced the interaction of IRAK2 with RanBP2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation experiments with phosphorylation site mutants.

claim: ALYREF and SRSF1 belong to the same family of proteins called the shuttling SR (serine- and arginine-rich) proteins, sharing a similar RNA-binding domain.
source: Notably, ALYREF and SRSF1 actually belong to the same family of proteins called the shuttling SR (serine- and arginine-rich) proteins, sharing a similar RNA-binding domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: SRSF1 and ALYREF can bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif.
source: Indeed, we found SRSF1 and ALYREF were able to bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from REMSA experiments showing both proteins bind the same motif.

claim: Removal of SRSF1 allows nuclear export adaptor ALYREF binding to target mRNAs.
source: Indeed, we found SRSF1 and ALYREF were able to bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif; and the removal of SRSF1 allowed nuclear export adaptor ALYREF binding to the target mRNAs
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from RNA immunoprecipitation experiments in SRSF1 knockdown cells.

claim: SRSF1-mediated nuclear sequestration of target mRNAs is achieved by blocking the binding of ALYREF to the mRNAs.
source: Indeed, we found SRSF1 and ALYREF were able to bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif; and the removal of SRSF1 allowed nuclear export adaptor ALYREF binding to the target mRNAs, suggesting that SRSF1-mediated nuclear sequestration of target mRNAs might be achieved by blocking the binding of ALYREF to the mRNAs.
evidence: This mechanism is inferred from the observation that SRSF1 and ALYREF bind the same motif and SRSF1 removal allows ALYREF binding.

claim: ALYREF (a subunit of the TREX complex) makes contact with nuclear export receptor Nxf1, serving as a bridge between mRNA and Nxf1.
source: Importantly, previous studies have reported that ALYREF (a subunit of the so-called TREX complex for nuclear export) makes contact with nuclear export receptor Nxf1, serving as a bridge between mRNA and nuclear export receptor Nxf1.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies about ALYREF function.

claim: Nuclear IRAK2 mediates removal of SRSF1 and facilitates assembly of nuclear export machinery to export inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for translation.
source: Thus, nuclear IRAK2 mediates the removal of SRSF1 and facilitates the assembly of nuclear export machinery to export the inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for translation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: About 10–30% of LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts are exported out of the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2.
source: Interestingly, about 10–30% LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts were exported out of the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2 (Figure 3B)
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 3B shows partial export of inflammatory transcripts in IRAK2 KO cells.

claim: There might be another mechanism besides IRAK2 that allows ALYREF binding to target mRNAs for nuclear export.
source: Interestingly, about 10–30% LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts were exported out of the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2 (Figure 3B), which was consistent with the residual ALYREF's binding to these transcripts in IRAK2-/- cells (Figure 4D). These results implicate that there might be yet another mechanism besides IRAK2 that allows ALYREF binding to the target mRNAs for nuclear export.
evidence: This possibility is inferred from the observation that some export occurs without IRAK2.
